passage:
Pooja, come here. You asked how I got through my first job? It was not easy, and I'm Usha. My section head, a big man, would shout in front of everyone: "Stupid girl, are you blind?" Once he threw my file on the floor. I froze every time, and started to think I was truly useless.
A colleague named Rekha sat me down. "This is not normal. Write it all down, dates, words, who was there." I did. Then, with Rekha beside me, I took my notes to the head of HR. She listened for an hour, said, "This is unacceptable, thank you for bringing it," and started a formal inquiry. He was warned in writing.

qa.q: What did the section head throw on the floor?
qa.a: The section head threw Usha's file on the floor.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling as the section head kept shouting in front of everyone?
qa.a: Usha felt frozen and began to doubt herself, coming to think she was useless. The shouting made it hard to answer back.

qa.q: What steps did Usha take that led to change?
qa.a: Usha wrote down dates, words and who was there, then took the notes to the head of HR with Rekha beside. That made the complaint clear and safe to bring.

qa.q: How did Rekha's response make a difference to Usha?
qa.a: Rekha said "This is not normal" and sat beside Usha in the HR office. Having an ally helped Usha see it was not her fault and act on it.

grounding: A person shouted at and belittled by a superior freezes and doubts themselves, then documents incidents, finds an ally and uses the formal channel, told by an elder.

passage:
Friday, 6:40 pm, the last hour before the month-end file was due. Devika, the branch manager, stood over Yusuf's desk. "Useless. Anyone could do this better. Do you want to keep this job?" The whole floor went quiet.
Yusuf's hands went cold, and he could not find the words. He finished the file, then sat in his car with the engine off, thinking maybe he really was useless.
Over the weekend he wrote down the date, time and words, and asked Imran, who had been nearby, whether he'd seen it. Imran said, "I did. I'll say so." On Monday Yusuf emailed the regional grievance officer, who replied the same day: "Thank you for reporting this. I will look into it and meet you on Wednesday."

qa.q: What time on Friday did Devika stand over Yusuf's desk?
qa.a: It was around 6:40 pm on Friday.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling after Devika's shouting, sitting in the car with the engine off?
qa.a: Yusuf felt shaken and began to doubt himself, thinking he might be useless. Cold hands and no words show how deeply the shouting hit.

qa.q: What steps did Yusuf take over the weekend and on Monday?
qa.a: Yusuf wrote down the date, time and words, asked Imran who had witnessed it and emailed the regional grievance officer. That used the formal channel instead of silence.

qa.q: What might it have meant to Yusuf that Imran said "I'll say so"?
qa.a: Imran's words probably meant Yusuf was not alone and was believed. It was one of the things that made reporting possible.

grounding: A person belittled by a superior in front of the floor freezes and doubts themselves, then documents it, finds an ally and reports through a formal channel, and the grievance officer replies.

passage:
"Aadhya, come, sit. You've been quiet all week. Is it your team lead again? Let Binita di tell you what happened to me.
"At twenty-four I worked under a man who shouted. Not at everyone. At me. 'Useless.' 'Even a child could do this.' In front of the whole floor. I would freeze. My mind went blank, and by evening I believed him.
"A senior, Mrs D'Souza, saw me crying on the stairs. She said, 'Start writing it down. Date, time, words, who was there.' So I did. Every night, in a small diary.
"Two colleagues had seen it too. They agreed to speak up if asked.
"After six weeks I took the diary to HR. The HR head read every page, thanked me, and started a formal inquiry that same week. She moved me to another team while it ran.
"Keeping quiet did not stop him, Aadhya. Writing it down and finding my people did.

qa.q: What did Mrs D'Souza tell young Binita to write down?
qa.a: She said, "Date, time, words, who was there."

qa.q: What was young Binita feeling after being shouted at?
qa.a: Young Binita felt frozen and ashamed, her mind going blank until she began to doubt herself and believe the insults.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Binita di's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Mrs D'Souza's advice to keep a written record, with colleagues willing to speak, gave her proof and allies to take to HR, which led to a formal inquiry.

qa.q: How did Mrs D'Souza likely feel seeing Binita on the stairs?
qa.a: Mrs D'Souza likely felt concern and sympathy, and wanted to protect the younger colleague.

grounding: An elder recalls being belittled by a boss and freezing, then documenting, finding allies and using formal channels.

passage:
It was a tight deadline week, and the team worked from home in three cities, the video calls freezing on bad Wi-Fi. On Tuesday's call, the manager, Mr Arora, cut Mehak off mid-sentence. "Did you even read the brief, or do you just guess? This is amateur work." Ten faces on screen. Mehak's camera froze on her stunned expression.
Afterwards she sat staring at the laptop. Maybe he was right. Maybe she was bad at this.
Her phone buzzed. Lalremsiami, a colleague: "That was not okay. I've heard him do it twice before. Are you alright?"
They talked that evening. Lalremsiami said, "Write it down while it's fresh." Mehak did: the date, the time, his exact words, the ten people present.
On Friday, after a second outburst, they both emailed HR. The HR manager called Mehak within an hour, listened, said it would be treated seriously and confidentially, and set a meeting for Monday.

qa.q: What did Mr Arora call Mehak's work?
qa.a: He called it "amateur work".

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling after the call?
qa.a: Mehak felt stunned and doubted herself, wondering whether she was really bad at the job.

qa.q: Which steps helped protect Mehak, and why?
qa.a: Writing down the date, time, words and witnesses, finding an ally in Lalremsiami, and emailing HR gave her a record and support instead of silence.

qa.q: How was Lalremsiami affected by what she saw?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt troubled and protective, having seen him do it before, and reached out to make sure Mehak was all right.

grounding: A person belittled by a superior freezes and doubts herself, then documents incidents, finds an ally and uses formal channels.

passage:
In the glass-walled meeting room of the Gurugram office, Deepak, the department head, threw Ira's report on the table. "Did you write this in your sleep? Pathetic." The team went silent. Ira felt her face burn. She couldn't speak.
For a week afterwards she rewrote every email three times and stopped suggesting ideas. At night she wondered if she was as useless as he said.
Her teammate Kunal found her in the pantry. "He did the same to me in March. You're not the problem."
That night Ira opened a document and wrote down each incident: the date, what Deepak said, who was in the room. There were four.
The office had an internal complaints policy she'd never read. She read it twice, then booked a meeting with HR, bringing the document and Kunal as a witness.
The HR manager listened, kept a copy, told her retaliation would not be tolerated, and opened a formal review that afternoon.

qa.q: How many incidents did Ira write down?
qa.a: There were four.

qa.q: How did Ira feel in the week after the meeting?
qa.a: Ira felt ashamed and doubtful, rewriting every email and wondering if she was as useless as Deepak said.

qa.q: Which steps protected Ira, and why?
qa.a: Documenting each incident, finding an ally in Kunal and using the formal complaints process gave her evidence and support, which staying silent would not.

qa.q: How did Kunal's own experience shape Kunal's response to Ira?
qa.a: Having been treated the same way in March, Kunal felt sympathy and wanted Ira to know she was not the problem.

grounding: A person belittled by a superior freezes and doubts herself, then documents incidents, finds an ally and uses formal channels.

passage:
"Are you stupid, Yash? A child could have built this sheet. Get out of my sight."
Alka's voice carried across the whole floor. Yash stood holding the laptop, mouth open, no words coming.
Later, at the water cooler, Meera touched his sleeve. "That's the third time this month."
"Maybe she's right. Maybe I am slow."
"You're not. The client praised that sheet last week. Do you have the dates?"
"Some. The 4th, the 12th, today."
"Write each one down tonight. What she said, who was there. I was there today and on the 12th. I'll put my name to it."
Two days later the HR manager read the pages slowly. "Thank you for the dates and the witness. This isn't something you fix by working harder. We're opening a formal review today, and until it's done you'll report to Rohit."
Yash let out a breath he felt he had been holding for a month.

qa.q: Which dates did Yash have?
qa.a: The 4th, the 12th, today.

qa.q: What does Yash's "Maybe I am slow" reveal?
qa.a: It reveals Yash was shaken and doubting himself after being belittled in front of the whole floor.

qa.q: Which steps protected Yash here?
qa.a: Writing down dates, words and witnesses, having an ally offer to be named as a witness, and taking it to HR, which opened a formal review and changed who he reports to.

qa.q: Why might Meera have stepped in at the water cooler?
qa.a: Meera had witnessed two of the incidents and was worried and uncomfortable watching Yash be belittled, so she offered to be a witness.

grounding: Shows a person shouted at and belittled by a superior who freezes and doubts himself, and is protected by records, an ally and a formal channel.
